excerpt: Key findings at a glance (482 live sites, 25 November 2026) Every percentage below is measured directly from live HTTP responses and public DNS TXT records on 25 November 2026. All findings are aggregated and anonymized; no individual domain is named. Check it now. The security headers checker reads a page’s HSTS, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, frame protection, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy; the indexability checker reads a page’s noindex, robots.txt, canonical address and redirects. No account, and the address is not stored. 1. HTTPS is universal, but 58.5% ship zero browser security headers All 482 responsive websites redirected or loaded over HTTPS (100.0%). Free automated TLS certificates have solved baseline transport encryption, yet response-level browser hardening has barely moved outside dedicated engineering teams. We checked five baseline headers recommended by the OWASP Secure Headers Project: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS), Content-Security-Policy (CSP), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, clickjacking protection (X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors), and Referrer-Policy. Per-header gaps across the 482 sites: - Missing Content-Security-Policy: 84.9% (409 sites) - Missing Referrer-Policy: 78.8% (380 sites) - Missing Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS): 75.9% (366 sites) - Missing clickjacking protection (X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors): 74.3% (358 sites) - Missing X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff: 69.3% (334 sites) - Version banner disclosure (Server: nginx/x.y or X-Powered-By): 31.3% (151 sites) Because 63.3% (305) of the cohort runs WordPress on managed or shared hosting, default server blocks rarely add HSTS, nosniff, or Referrer-Policy unless an agency configures them at the reverse proxy or CDN edge.
